The work reported in Munguía-López et al. quantified carbon footprint, energy use, and water consumption for multiple STRAP process configurations (Munguía-López et al., 2023b). We found that STRAP configurations leveraging temperature-based precipitation (without the use of antisolvents) offer the best environmental advantages relative to virgin multilayer film production, which is an improvement to prior models We deployed our STRAP process models for key industrial applications, including the recycling of high- purity polypropylene from disposable face masks,(Yu et al., 2023) recycling of single-use multilayer plastics for biomanufacturing,(Tushar et al., 2025) and recycling of post- industrial printed multilayer plastic films containing polyurethane inks (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023). As part of this work, we have also developed a fast and automated framework to identify optimal strategies to recycle multi-layer films with many layers using STRAP (which involves solvent selection); we have also extended these results to identify green solvents to conduct separations (Ikegwu, Munguía-López, et al., 2025; Ikegwu, Zhou, et al., 2025). As part of Subtask 2.1.3 we conducted system-wide studied to understand conditions under which waste feedstocks follow distinct pathways (Erickson et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2023; Olafasakin, Ma, Bradshaw, et al., 2023). For example, in Ma et al. we developed a holistic optimization framework that integrates supply chain analysis, techno-economic analysis, and life-cycle analysis for investigating the economic viability and environmental benefits of upcycling infrastructures that collect, sort, clean, and process post-consumer plastic waste for producing virgin polymer resins (Ma et al., 2023). We demonstrated that coordinated collection, sorting, and conversion systems could achieve economic viability at regional scale. We have also extended this analysis to a national scale (Erickson et al., 2024); our models are open source and general and can be used to analyze diverse scenarios in different regions and under different policy conditions. For instance, our models have been recently used to conduct studies in Spain (García et al., 2026). We have also put together a comprehensive superstructure optimization framework that automatically determines how a certain feedstock will be routed to STRAP or thermal decomposition depending on its decomposition. For Task 3.1, we sought to inform process-level modeling and decision-making for solvent selection and process design by coupling experimentally measured material properties, molecular modeling for predicting solubilities, and advanced optimization and machine learning. We have applied these methodologies in the context of the STRAP process and for pyrolysis systems. Under Subtask 3.1.1, we developed a database architecture to capture rheological behavior, mechanical performance, and analytical descriptors relevant to recycled polymers. This database contains data collected in diverse studies conducted in the CUWP project. For instance, we collected data from the work of ISU team in which they demonstrated that polymers recovered via STRAP from multilayer packaging films retain material properties suitable for reuse (Cecon et al., 2022).
